Description: implicit — serverless tile hosting on GitHub Pages
prompt: I want to host map tiles on GitHub Pages without running any backend. Is that possible with MapLibre GL JS?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Yes – you can serve a complete tile set from a GitHub Pages site with no server-side code at all.** The trick is to use **PMTiles**, a single-file archive that the browser reads with HTTP Range requests. GitHub Pages (any static host that supports `Range` and CORS) will serve the file exactly the way MapLibre needs it. Below is a complete, step-by-step guide: --- ## 1. Why PMTiles (and not MBTiles?) | Feature | MBTiles | **PMTiles** | |---------|---------|-------------| | Single file archive | ✅ | ✅ | | Can be read with plain HTTP Range requests (no special server) | ❌ – the client would need a server that understands the SQLite format | **✅ – the client fetches byte ranges directly** | | Works with the `pmtiles://` protocol handler that MapLibre provides | ❌ – you would need a tile server | **✅ – just add the protocol once** | | Works on GitHub Pages, S3, Cloudflare R2, Netlify, Vercel, etc. | ❌ – static hosts can’t serve SQLite rows | **✅ – any static host that returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes`** | So the workflow is: 1. **Generate a `.pmtiles` file** (vector, raster, or raster-dem). 2. **Commit it to a GitHub repo** (or push it with Git LFS if it’s > 100 MiB). 3. **Enable GitHub Pages** for that repo (or a `gh-pages` branch). 4. **Reference the file in your MapLibre style** using the `pmtiles://` protocol. --- ## 2. Create the PMTiles archive ### 2.1 From existing MBTiles (quickest) ```bash # Install the official CLI (download the binary for your OS) # https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases pmtiles convert mytiles.mbtiles mytiles.pmtiles ``` ### 2.2 Directly from source data (tippecanoe example) ```bash # tippecanoe ≥ 2.17 can write PMTiles directly tippecanoe -zg -o mytiles.pmtiles mydata.geojson ``` ### 2.3 From OSM with Planetiler (global or regional basemap) ```bash java -jar planetiler.jar --download --area=monaco --output=monaco.pmtiles ``` > **Tip:** Run `pmtiles show mytiles.pmtiles --metadata` to verify the layer names (`vector_layers`) and the zoom range before you upload. --- ## 3. Put the file on GitHub Pages ### 3.1 Size limits | GitHub Pages limit | What to do if you exceed it | |--------------------|-----------------------------| | **≤ 100 MiB** – normal file in the repo | Just commit the file. | | **> 100 MiB** – must use **Git LFS** (or split the archive) | 1. `git lfs install`
2. `git lfs track "*.pmtiles"`
3. `git add mytiles.pmtiles`
4. `git commit …`
5. Push – GitHub will store the file in LFS and serve it transparently from the Pages site. | > **Important:** Git LFS files are still served with `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so the PMTiles client works unchanged. ### 3.2 Repository layout (example) ``` my-map-repo/ │ ├─ index.html ← your page that creates the MapLibre map ├─ style.json ← MapLibre style (see §4) ├─ mytiles.pmtiles ← the tile archive (or LFS pointer) └─ .gitattributes ← (optional) `*.pmtiles filter=lfs diff=lfs merge=lfs -text` ``` ### 3.3 Enable Pages 1. In the repo → **Settings → Pages**. 2. Choose the branch (`main` or `gh-pages`) and the root folder (`/`). 3. Click **Save**. GitHub will give you a URL like `https://username.github.io/my-map-repo/`. That URL is now a static web server that: * Serves `mytiles.pmtiles` with `Accept-Ranges: bytes`. * Sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (so cross-origin fetches succeed). You can verify with `curl -I`: ```bash curl -I https://username.github.io/my-map-repo/mytiles.pmtiles # → should contain: # Accept-Ranges: bytes # Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * ``` --- ## 4. Wire the archive into MapLibre GL JS ### 4.1 Install the PMTiles protocol library ```bash npm install pmtiles maplibre-gl # or use a CDN for a quick demo: # # ``` ### 4.2 Register the protocol **once** (e.g. in a module that runs before any map is created) ```js import * as pmtiles from 'pmtiles'; import * as maplibregl from 'maplibre-gl'; // Create the protocol handler const protocol = new pmtiles.Protocol(); // Register it globally – this works for MapLibre v3, v4, v5, v6 maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', protocol.tile); ``` > **Why the global registration?** > `addProtocol` stores the handler in a static registry. Registering it a single time (e.g. in your app’s entry point or a React context provider) guarantees that every map on the page can resolve `pmtiles://…` URLs. ### 4.3 Style that points at the archive ```json { "version": 8, "sources": { "mytiles": { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://username.github.io/my-map-repo/mytiles.pmtiles" } }, "layers": [ { "id": "water", "type": "fill", "source": "mytiles", "source-layer": "water", // <-- name from `vector_layers` metadata "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" } }, { "id": "roads", "type": "line", "source": "mytiles", "source-layer": "road", "paint": { "line-color": "#777", "line-width": 1 } } // …add more layers as you like ] } ``` **Key points** * **Use `url:`**, not `tiles:`. The PMTiles protocol reads the archive header and automatically supplies `minzoom`, `maxzoom`, `bounds`, etc. If you use `tiles: ['pmtiles://…/{z}/{x}/{y}']` you lose that information and MapLibre will assume a default `maxzoom: 22`, causing unnecessary 404s at higher zooms. * The `source-layer` values must match the `id` fields in the archive’s `vector_layers` metadata. Run `pmtiles show mytiles.pmtiles --metadata` to list them. * For **raster** or **raster-dem** archives, change `"type": "raster"` (or `"raster-dem"`) and add `"encoding": "terrarium"` for DEMs. ### 4.4 Minimal HTML page ```html PMTiles on GitHub Pages
``` Deploy this `index.html`, `style.json`, and `mytiles.pmtiles` to the same repo, push, and the map will work instantly. --- ## 5. Common pitfalls & how to fix them | Symptom | Likely cause | Fix | |---------|--------------|-----| | **Blank vector tiles** (no features) | Using `tiles:` instead of `url:` → MapLibre thinks the archive has a higher `maxzoom` and requests zoom levels that don’t exist. | Switch to `url:` as shown in §4.3. | | **CORS error** (`No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header`) | The file is being served from a different domain that doesn’t send CORS headers (e.g., a private S3 bucket). | GitHub Pages already sends `*`. If you host elsewhere, configure the bucket or CDN to add `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. | | **Range request not honored** (`206 Partial Content` missing) | Host does not support `Range` (some cheap static hosts). | GitHub Pages, S3, Cloudflare R2, Netlify, Vercel all support it. Switch to one of those. | | **File > 100 MiB and not loading** | Uploaded as a normal Git object (GitHub Pages truncates it). | Use **Git LFS** for the `.pmtiles` file, or split the archive with `pmtiles extract`. | | **MapLibre v4+ throws “tile data missing”** | You wrote a custom protocol handler that returns a raw `ArrayBuffer` instead of `{data: …}`. | Use the built-in `protocol.tile` from the `pmtiles` library (it already returns the correct `{data}` shape). | | **Layer names don’t match** | You guessed the `source-layer` names. | Run `pmtiles show mytiles.pmtiles --metadata` and copy the exact `id` values from the `vector_layers` array. | --- ## 6. Optional: Split a huge global archive If your dataset is > 2 GiB or you want faster initial load, you can create **regional PMTiles** and load the appropriate one with a *source selector*: ```json { "sources": { "europe": { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://username.github.io/tiles/europe.pmtiles", "bounds": [ -10, 35, 30, 70 ] // optional, helps MapLibre pick the right source }, "asia": { "type": "vector", "url": "pmtiles://https://username.github.io/tiles/asia.pmtiles", "bounds": [ 60, -10, 150, 55 ] } }, "layers": [ /* same layers, but each source can be used conditionally */ ] } ``` MapLibre will request tiles from the source whose bounds contain the current view. This pattern keeps each file under the GitHub Pages size limit and improves cache locality. --- ##

Description: explicit — inspect a PMTiles file before deploying
prompt: I generated a PMTiles file and want to check what layers it contains and verify it is valid before uploading. How?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
Below is a **step-by-step checklist** you can run on your workstation to

1. **List the vector (or raster) layers that are inside the archive** – so you know what `source-layer` names to use in your MapLibre style.  
2. **Validate the file structure** – catch missing offsets, corrupted tiles, wrong header values, etc., before you push the file to S3, R2, GitHub Pages, …  

Everything is done with the **official `pmtiles` CLI** (the same binary that the Protomaps library uses). No extra code, no network traffic, and it works on macOS, Linux and Windows.

---

## 1️⃣ Install the CLI (once)

| OS | Command |
|----|---------|
| macOS (brew) | `brew install protomaps/tap/pmtiles` |
| Linux (deb/ rpm) | Download the appropriate binary from the [GitHub releases page](https://github.com/protomaps/go-pmtiles/releases) and put it on your `$PATH`. |
| Windows | Grab `pmtiles-windows-amd64.exe`, rename to `pmtiles.exe` and add the folder to your `PATH`. |
| Docker (any OS) | `docker run --rm -v "$(pwd)":/data protomaps/go-pmtiles:latest <command>` (replace `<command>` with the examples below). |

> **Tip:** The current stable CLI version is `v3.x`. All the commands shown work on any `v3` release (and on newer `v4` when they appear).

---

## 2️⃣ Quick sanity-check: `show`

```bash
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles
```

**What you get**

```
type:               vector
tile_type:          mvt
bounds:             -180.0,-85.0511,180.0,85.0511
minzoom:            0
maxzoom:            14
tile_count:         1 234 567
metadata:           <object, use --metadata to view full JSON metadata>
```

*If the file is raster* you’ll see `type: raster` (or `raster-dem`) and the same set of header fields.

**Why it matters**

* `minzoom` / `maxzoom` – MapLibre will automatically use these when you reference the archive with `url:` (not `tiles:`).  
* `bounds` – useful for clipping or for deciding whether you need to split the archive.  
* `tile_count` – sanity-check that the file isn’t empty or unexpectedly huge.

---

## 3️⃣ List the **layer names** (the values you’ll use for `source-layer`)

The plain `show` output only tells you that there is a metadata object.  
To see the actual layer list you must ask for the JSON metadata:

```bash
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata
```

Typical JSON fragment for a **vector** archive:

```json
{
  "vector_layers": [
    { "id": "water",        "fields": { "class": "String", "name": "String" } },
    { "id": "roads",        "fields": { "class": "String", "ref": "String" } },
    { "id": "buildings",    "fields": { "height": "Number", "type": "String" } },
    { "id": "landuse",      "fields": { "class": "String" } }
  ],
  "name": "my-region-basemap",
  "description": "Vector tiles generated with tippecanoe",
  "format": "pbf",
  "attribution": "© OpenStreetMap contributors"
}
```

*The `id` values are exactly what you write in the style:*

```json
{
  "id": "water",
  "type": "fill",
  "source": "myPmtiles",
  "source-layer": "water",
  "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" }
}
```

If the archive is **raster** or **raster-dem**, the metadata will contain a `raster_layers` array (or may be empty). The layer name is still the `id` field, but raster sources ignore `source-layer` – you just reference the source.

---

## 4️⃣ Full integrity verification

```bash
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles
```

**Possible outcomes**

| Exit code | Message | Meaning |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| `0` | `✅ verification succeeded` | The header offsets, tile lengths, zoom-range table, and internal checksums are all consistent. |
| `1` | `❌ verification failed: <reason>` | Something is broken – e.g. a tile offset points outside the file, a tile length is wrong, duplicate tile keys, or the file ends prematurely. |

If verification fails, the CLI prints a short description (e.g. “tile offset for z=5,x=12,y=7 points beyond EOF”). In that case you should **re-run the generation step** (or run `pmtiles extract` on a known-good source to rebuild a smaller file).

> **Note:** `verify` does **not** decode the tile payloads (it doesn’t check that a vector tile is valid protobuf). It only checks the archive structure, which is what most upload pipelines need. If you also want to be sure the tiles themselves are parseable, you can fetch a single tile with `pmtiles tile` (see next section) and pipe it through `mapbox-vector-tile` or `gdalinfo` for raster.

---

## 5️⃣ (Optional) Peek at a single tile – useful for debugging layer names or geometry

```bash
# Grab tile z=5,x=12,y=7 and write it to a file
pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 5/12/7 > tile.pbf
```

*For raster archives* the output will be a PNG/JPEG/WEBP file; you can open it with any image viewer.

*For vector archives* you can inspect the protobuf with a tiny Node script or with `vt2geojson`:

```bash
npm install -g @mapbox/vector-tile-js vt2geojson
vt2geojson tile.pbf > tile.geojson
```

Now you can see the exact feature properties and confirm that the `source-layer` you plan to use actually contains data at that zoom.

---

## 6️⃣ Putting it all together – a one-liner checklist

```bash
# 1️⃣ Show header (quick sanity)
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles

# 2️⃣ List layer names (what you’ll use in the style)
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata | jq '.vector_layers[].id'

# 3️⃣ Verify archive integrity
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles

# 4️⃣ (optional) Grab a sample tile to double-check geometry
pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 5/12/7 > sample.pbf
vt2geojson sample.pbf | head
```

If **all three commands succeed** (header prints, layer list is what you expect, verification returns exit code 0), you can safely upload the file to your static host.

---

## 7️⃣ Common pitfalls & how to fix them

| Symptom | Likely cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| `pmtiles show` prints “metadata: <object, use --metadata …>” but `--metadata` returns **empty** or missing `vector_layers` | The archive was built without a proper TileJSON `vector_layers` entry (some older tippecanoe versions omitted it). | Regenerate the tiles with `--layer` flags or add the metadata later with `pmtiles edit mydata.pmtiles --metadata='{"vector_layers":[...]}’`. |
| `pmtiles verify` fails with “tile offset points beyond EOF” | The file was truncated during upload (e.g. GitHub Pages has a 100 MB limit) or the download was incomplete. | Re-upload the full file (use S3, R2, or a CDN that accepts >100 MB). |
| MapLibre shows **blank vector tiles** even though the CLI shows layers | The style used `tiles:` instead of `url:` or the `source-layer` name is misspelled. | Use `url: "pmtiles://https://…/mydata.pmtiles"` and double-check the `source-layer` strings against the `vector_layers` list. |
| CORS error when loading from S3 | The bucket does not return `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` or `Accept-Ranges`. | In the S3 bucket properties enable **CORS** with a rule that allows `GET` and the `Range` header, e.g.:

```xml
<CORSRule>
  <AllowedOrigin>*</AllowedOrigin>
  <AllowedMethod>GET</AllowedMethod>
  <AllowedHeader>Range</AllowedHeader>
  <ExposeHeader>Accept-Ranges</ExposeHeader>
</CORSRule>
```

|  |  |

---

## 8️⃣ Quick “cheat-sheet” for copy-and-paste

```bash
# -------------------------------------------------
# 1️⃣ Header & basic stats
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles

# -------------------------------------------------
# 2️⃣ Full metadata (layer names)
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles --metadata | jq '.vector_layers'

# -------------------------------------------------
# 3️⃣ Verify archive integrity
pmtiles verify mydata.pmtiles

# -------------------------------------------------
# 4️⃣ Sample tile (optional)
pmtiles tile mydata.pmtiles 5/12/7 > sample.pbf
#   → inspect with vt2geojson or any vector-tile viewer
```

---

### TL;DR

*Run `pmtiles show … --metadata` to see the exact `source-layer` IDs.*  
*Run `pmtiles verify …` to be 100 % sure the file isn’t corrupted.*  
*If both succeed, you’re ready to upload the `.pmtiles` file to any static host that supports HTTP range requests and CORS.*  

Happy mapping! 🚀

Description: negative — wrong tool for live PostGIS data
prompt: I'm building a map that shows bus positions updating every 30 seconds from a PostGIS database. Should I use PMTiles?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:** No – PMTiles is a *static* archive format. It’s perfect when you want to serve a fixed set of tiles (vector or raster) from a simple static host, but it can’t be updated on the fly. A bus-position layer that changes every 30 seconds needs a live data source (or a tile server that can rebuild tiles on demand).

Below is a quick decision matrix, the reasons why PMTiles isn’t a fit for your use-case, and a few practical alternatives that work well with MapLibre GL JS.

---

## 1️⃣ Why PMTiles isn’t suitable for live bus positions

| Feature | PMTiles | Live bus-position feed |
|---------|---------|------------------------|
| **Data mutability** | Immutable once the file is written. You would have to rewrite the whole `.pmtiles` file (or a large chunk of it) every time the data changes. | Data changes continuously; you want to push new points every 30 s. |
| **Update latency** | You’d need to rebuild the archive, upload it, and wait for the CDN to propagate – minutes to hours. | You need sub-minute latency. |
| **Client-side expectations** | MapLibre treats a PMTiles source as a TileJSON that describes a fixed min/max-zoom, bounds, and layer schema. It never asks the server for “new tiles” unless the zoom/pan changes. | The client must request the *latest* geometry for the same tile coordinates over and over. |
| **Server requirements** | Only a static host that supports HTTP Range (S3, Cloudflare R2, GitHub Pages, etc.). No server-side logic. | You need a server that can query PostGIS (or another live store) and return fresh tiles or features on each request. |

Because of these constraints, trying to “rewrite the PMTiles file every 30 s” would be wasteful, error-prone, and would defeat the whole point of using a static-file format.

---

## 2️⃣ Recommended approaches for a rapidly-changing point layer

### A. **GeoJSON (or NDJSON) source with polling**
```js
const map = new maplibregl.Map({ /* … */ });

map.addSource('buses', {
  type: 'geojson',
  data: 'https://example.com/api/buses', // returns FeatureCollection
  // optional: enable clustering, maxzoom, buffer, etc.
});

map.addLayer({
  id: 'bus-points',
  type: 'circle',
  source: 'buses',
  paint: {
    'circle-radius': 6,
    'circle-color': '#ff6600',
    'circle-stroke-width': 1,
    'circle-stroke-color': '#fff'
  }
});

// Simple 30-second poll
setInterval(async () => {
  const resp = await fetch('https://example.com/api/buses');
  const geojson = await resp.json();
  map.getSource('buses').setData(geojson);
}, 30_000);
```
*Pros*:  
- Very easy to implement.  
- No tile generation step; you just return the latest points as GeoJSON.  

*Cons*:  
- Not ideal for very large numbers of points (tens of thousands) because the whole payload is sent each poll.  
- No built-in tile-level caching; every request hits your API.

### B. **Vector tiles generated on demand (Tile Server)**
1. **Set up a lightweight vector-tile server** that reads directly from PostGIS and serves TileJSON/XYZ or MVT tiles. Popular choices:
   - **[Martin](https://github.com/maplibre/martin)** – a Go server that can read PostGIS, MBTiles, or PMTiles. It supports the `?access_token=` style and can be run behind a CDN.
   - **[t-rex](https://github.com/t-rex-tileserver/t-rex)** – also Go-based, fast, supports PostGIS, and can serve vector tiles with caching.
   - **[tileserver-gl](https://github.com/maptiler/tileserver-gl)** – Node-based, can read MBTiles/PMTiles *or* generate tiles from a PostGIS connection via `pg_tileserv` (see below).
   - **[pg_tileserv](https://github.com/CrunchyData/pg_tileserv)** – a tiny Go server that turns any PostGIS table into a TileJSON + MVT endpoint with zero configuration.

2. **Expose an endpoint** like `https://tiles.example.com/bus/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf`. The server will query PostGIS for the points that intersect the tile’s bounding box and return an MVT (Mapbox Vector Tile) on each request.

3. **Add the source in MapLibre** (using the `url` property so the TileJSON header is read automatically):
   ```js
   map.addSource('buses', {
     type: 'vector',
     url: 'pmtiles://https://tiles.example.com/bus.json' // if you expose TileJSON via /bus.json
     // or, without PMTiles protocol:
     // url: 'https://tiles.example.com/bus.json'
   });

   map.addLayer({
     id: 'bus-points',
     type: 'circle',
     source: 'buses',
     'source-layer': 'bus', // name of the layer inside the MVT
     paint: { 'circle-color': '#ff6600', 'circle-radius': 5 }
   });
   ```

*Pros*:  
- Only the tiles that the client actually needs are sent (tiny MVTs).  
- Scales to many thousands of points because each tile contains only the subset that falls inside it.  
- You can keep the same endpoint for any zoom level; the server does the heavy lifting.

*Cons*:  
- You need to run a small server (still “serverless-ish” if you host it on a cheap VPS, Cloud Run, or Lambda with a warm container).  
- Slightly more ops than a pure static host, but the server is trivial compared to a full-blown tile rendering stack.

### C. **Hybrid: static basemap + live overlay**
If you already have a static basemap in PMTiles (e.g., a country-level OSM vector basemap), you can **combine** it with a live overlay:

```js
// Basemap source (static PMTiles)
map.addSource('basemap', {
  type: 'vector',
  url: 'pmtiles://https://example.com/basemap.pmtiles'
});

// Live bus source (GeoJSON or tile server)
map.addSource('buses', { /* see A or B */ });
```

This gives you the best of both worlds: a fast, CDN-cached basemap and a dynamic overlay.

---

## 3️⃣ Quick “starter kit” if you want to go with a tile server

Below is a minimal Docker-compose setup using **pg_tileserv** (the simplest way to expose PostGIS tables as vector tiles). Adjust the `POSTGRES_*` env vars to point at your existing DB.

```yaml
version: '3.8'
services:
  db:
    image: postgis/postgis:15-3.3
    environment:
      POSTGRES_USER: mapuser
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: secret
      POSTGRES_DB: maps
    volumes:
      - ./init.sql:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d/init.sql  # load your bus table
    ports: ["5432:5432"]

  tileserv:
    image: crunchydata/pg_tileserv:latest
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://mapuser:secret@db:5432/maps?sslmode=disable
    ports: ["7800:7800"]
    depends_on: [db]
```

`init.sql` could contain something like:

```sql
CREATE TABLE bus_positions (
  id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  vehicle_id TEXT,
  geom GEOMETRY(Point, 3857),   -- store in Web Mercator for fast tile queries
  ts TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE DEFAULT now()
);
-- Index for fast tile queries
CREATE INDEX bus_geom_idx ON bus_positions USING GIST (geom);
```

Now `http://localhost:7800/bus_positions` returns a TileJSON, and `http://localhost:7800/bus_positions/{z}/{x}/{y}.pbf` serves MVT tiles that always reflect the current rows in the table. Just keep the `bus_positions` table refreshed (e.g., a background job that inserts the latest GPS fixes every 30 s).

**MapLibre side:**

```js
map.addSource('buses', {
  type: 'vector',
  url: 'https://your-host.com/bus_positions' // TileJSON endpoint
});

map.addLayer({
  id: 'bus-points',
  type: 'circle',
  source: 'buses',
  'source-layer': 'bus_positions', // matches the table name
  paint: {
    'circle-color': '#ff6600',
    'circle-radius': 5,
    'circle-stroke-width': 1,
    'circle-stroke-color': '#fff'
  }
});
```

That’s it – the server will automatically query the latest rows each time a tile is requested.

---

## 4️⃣ TL;DR checklist for your bus-position map

| ✅ | Item |
|----|------|
| ❌ | **Do not** use PMTiles for a layer that changes every 30 s. |
| ✅ | Keep any static basemap (roads, terrain, etc.) in PMTiles if you like the zero-ops deployment model. |
| ✅ | Serve the live bus points via **one** of the following: |
|   | • **GeoJSON source** with a 30-s poll (good for < 5 k points). |
|   | • **Vector-tile server** (`pg_tileserv`, `t-rex`, `Martin`, etc.) that reads directly from PostGIS (scales to tens of thousands of points). |
| ✅ | Add the live source to your MapLibre style using `type: 'vector'` (or `type: 'geojson'` if you go the GeoJSON route). |
| ✅ | If you need a basemap, keep it in a PMTiles file and register the `pmtiles://` protocol once at app startup. |
| ✅ | Ensure CORS headers (`Access-Control-Allow-Origin:*`) on both the static PMTiles host and the tile server / API endpoint. |
| ✅ | Set appropriate cache-control on the static PMTiles file (e.g., `max-age=31536000`). The live tile server should use short-lived cache (or `Cache-Control: no-store`) so each request hits the DB. |

---

### Bottom line

**PMTiles = static, immutable archives.**  
**Live bus positions = dynamic, frequently updated data.**  

Use a live vector-tile endpoint (or a simple GeoJSON poll) for the bus layer, and optionally pair it with a static PMTiles basemap if you want the convenience of a single-file, CDN-cached background map. This gives you the best performance, the simplest architecture, and the correct semantics for a constantly moving fleet. Happy mapping! 🚍🗺️

Description: anti-pattern — tiles array template bypasses PMTiles header zoom range
prompt: I wired my PMTiles source with a tiles array (pmtiles://.../{z}/{x}/{y}) instead of url, and past a certain zoom the tiles go blank. The file is fine in pmtiles show. Why?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
**Short answer:**  
When you point a vector (or raster) source at a **`tiles:` array** like  

```json
"tiles": ["pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"]
```

MapLibre treats the source as a *regular* XYZ tile source. It **does not read the PM-Tiles header**, so it never learns the archive’s real `minzoom` / `maxzoom`.  
MapLibre therefore falls back to the default `maxzoom: 22`. As soon as the map asks for a zoom level that is **higher than the archive actually contains**, the PM-Tiles file returns “no tile” (the range request points past the end of the file). The client receives an empty tile and draws nothing – you see a blank map.

The file itself is fine (you can see the correct zoom range with `pmtiles show`), but the style is asking for tiles that simply aren’t in the archive.

---

## What’s happening under the hood

| Step | When you use `url:` (the recommended way) | When you use `tiles:` |
|------|--------------------------------------------|-----------------------|
| 1️⃣ MapLibre creates the source | Calls the **PMTiles protocol handler** (`pmtiles://…`) with the *archive URL* only. | Calls the protocol handler for each tile URL it builds (`…/z/x/y`). |
| 2️⃣ Protocol reads the archive header | The handler reads the PMTiles **header** (minzoom, maxzoom, bounds, vector_layers, etc.) and returns a **TileJSON** object that contains those values. | No header is read; the handler just serves the raw tile bytes for the exact URL you gave it. |
| 3️⃣ MapLibre knows the zoom range | `minzoom`/`maxzoom` from the header are stored in the source. Over-zooming beyond `maxzoom` is automatically handled by the client (it re-uses the highest-available tiles). | The source has **no zoom-range information** (the spec only allows `minzoom`/`maxzoom` to be set manually). The default `maxzoom` is **22**. |
| 4️⃣ Tile request | If the map asks for zoom > archive-max, the client **over-zooms** (re-uses the highest-available tiles) – no network request. | The client still asks the server for the exact `{z}/{x}/{y}` tile. The PMTiles file returns “no data” because that zoom level isn’t stored, so the tile is blank. |

That is why you see tiles up to the archive’s max zoom and then a sudden “blank” area.

---

## How to fix it

### 1. Use the `url:` property (recommended)

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "url": "pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles"
}
```

* The PMTiles protocol will read the header, inject the correct `minzoom`/`maxzoom`, and MapLibre will over-zoom automatically.
* You can still reference any `source-layer` inside the file; you do **not** need a `tiles:` array at all.

### 2. If you really need a `tiles:` array, set the zoom limits yourself

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": ["pmtiles://https://example.com/data.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14   // <-- set to the archive’s maxzoom (check with `pmtiles show`)
}
```

* This tells MapLibre not to request zoom levels higher than 14.
* You lose the automatic over-zoom behaviour (the client will still request the highest-available tiles, but you have to keep the numbers in sync).

### 3. Verify the archive’s zoom range

```bash
pmtiles show mydata.pmtiles
# Example output (excerpt)
{
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14,
  "bounds": [-180,-85,180,85],
  "vector_layers": [...]
}
```

Make sure the `maxzoom` you set in the style matches the value shown here.

### 4. Double-check CORS & Range support (just in case)

* The host must return `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and allow `Range` requests.
* It must also send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` (or your domain).  
  If the request fails, the protocol will return an empty tile, which looks the same as “zoom-out-of-range”.

---

## Quick checklist

| ✅ | What to verify |
|---|----------------|
| **Source definition** | Use `url:` (or set `maxzoom` manually if you must use `tiles:`). |
| **Protocol registration** | `maplibregl.addProtocol('pmtiles', new pmtiles.Protocol().tile);` – done **once** before any map is created. |
| **Archive header** | `pmtiles show <file>` → note `minzoom` / `maxzoom`. |
| **CORS & Range** | Host returns `Accept-Ranges: bytes` and `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. |
| **Cache headers** (optional) | `Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000` for immutable files. |
| **Over-zoom behaviour** | With `url:` you get automatic over-zoom; with `tiles:` you must limit `maxzoom`. |

---

## Example – the “fixed” style

```json
{
  "version": 8,
  "sources": {
    "world": {
      "type": "vector",
      "url": "pmtiles://https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/world.pmtiles"
    }
  },
  "layers": [
    {
      "id": "water",
      "type": "fill",
      "source": "world",
      "source-layer": "water",
      "paint": { "fill-color": "#a0c8f0" }
    },
    {
      "id": "roads",
      "type": "line",
      "source": "world",
      "source-layer": "road",
      "paint": { "line-color": "#777", "line-width": 1 }
    }
  ]
}
```

If you *must* keep a `tiles:` array (e.g., you’re mixing with other XYZ sources), add the explicit limits:

```json
{
  "type": "vector",
  "tiles": ["pmtiles://https://my-bucket.s3.amazonaws.com/world.pmtiles/{z}/{x}/{y}"],
  "minzoom": 0,
  "maxzoom": 14   // <-- matches the archive header
}
```

---

### TL;DR

*`tiles:` bypasses the PMTiles header → MapLibre assumes `maxzoom: 22` → requests zoom levels that don’t exist → blank tiles.*  
Switch to `url:` (or manually set `maxzoom`) and the problem disappears.
